resources.string: Warmth for cramps
Try a warm shower or a hot-water bottle wrapped in a towel on your abdomen.
Gentle movement
Walking, swimming or gentle yoga may ease period pain. Choose movement that feels comfortable.
Pain that interrupts your day
Book a medical appointment if pain limits daily activities, occurs during sex, or accompanies bleeding between periods.
Severe pelvic pain
Seek urgent medical care if pelvic pain is severe or worse than usual and painkillers have not helped.
When your head hurts
Drink water, eat regularly, relax and take a screen break. Avoid alcohol. Persistent or recurring headaches need medical review.
Headache: urgent signs
Get emergency help for a sudden extremely painful headache, weakness, confusion, speech trouble, loss of vision, or high fever with a stiff neck.
Find your headache pattern
Record when headaches start and possible triggers. A diary can help at a medical appointment; the app cannot determine the cause.
Ibuprofen · 18+

Check suitability first: ulcers, NSAID allergy, asthma, heart/kidney/liver disease, clotting problems, pregnancy or trying to conceive. Ask about other medicines, especially anticoagulants. Do not combine with naproxen or aspirin. Seek advice during breastfeeding.

Standard adult immediate-release tablets: 200–400 mg with food, up to 3 times daily; at least 4 hours apart. Maximum 1,200 mg in 24 hours without prescription. Use the smallest effective dose briefly; seek advice if pain persists, worsens or you need more than 10 days.
Paracetamol · 18+

Ask a pharmacist first for weight under 50 kg, liver/kidney disease, heavy alcohol use, other medicines or allergy. Do not combine products containing paracetamol. Overdose needs urgent medical advice, even if you feel well.

Standard adult tablets: 500–1,000 mg per dose; at least 4 hours apart. Maximum 4 doses and 4,000 mg in 24 hours. Do not use for more than 3 days without medical advice. Your product or health circumstances may require a lower limit.
Is bleeding heavy?
Changing protection every 1–2 hours, bleeding over 7 days or large clots are reasons to discuss your periods with a clinician.
Bleeding and fatigue
Heavy bleeding with fatigue or breathlessness deserves medical review. Blood tests may check for anaemia. Do not start iron or bleeding treatments solely from app logs.
Sleep, meals and stress
Regular movement, balanced meals, enough sleep and relaxation may help premenstrual symptoms. Seek support if symptoms affect daily life.
Track how you feel
Keep symptom notes for at least two cycles and bring them to an appointment. Timing alone does not establish PMS.
Before taking supplements
Evidence for PMS supplements is limited. Check with a clinician or pharmacist before adding them, especially alongside medicines.
If contraception failed

If pregnancy is unwanted and sex was unprotected or contraception failed, contact a pharmacist or clinic promptly. Emergency options have 3–5-day windows; sooner is better. A no-condom tag alone does not establish pregnancy risk.
Condoms and protection
Use a new condom each time and follow its instructions. With latex, use water- or silicone-based lubricant, not oil. If it breaks or slips, ask promptly about emergency contraception and STI testing.
When to take a pregnancy test

If pregnancy is possible, test from the first missed period. If the due date is unknown, test at least 21 days after unprotected sex. A negative test with continuing concern may need repeating and medical advice.
A late period has many causes

Pregnancy, stress, weight changes, contraception and other conditions can change timing. Seek medical advice after three missed periods in a row, or sooner for concerning symptoms. App dates cannot diagnose the cause.
